note: Written to be spoken: one sentence or phrase per line; {"beat": s} is a deliberate pause; code is spelled the way it is said. `answer` plays after the learner answers a predict step.

lines: Welcome to Data Structures and Algorithms.
Before any structure, the language its costs are written in.
A claim like... quicksort is n log n... hides three choices.
Which bound? Which case? And which resource?
Most arguments about complexity are really arguments about which one was meant.
All familiar? Swipe on.
Big O, big Omega, and Theta are inequalities.
Pick two constants, and a threshold... and the inequality must hold for every size past it.
Here, three n squared plus ten n sits between three n squared and four n squared... from ten onward.
At nine, it's three hundred thirty three. Just above the line.
The constants can't depend on n. That's the whole trick.
Two to the n plus one is big O of two to the n. Double it, and you're done.
But is two to the two n also big O of two to the n?
answer: No. Two to the two n is four to the n... and dividing by two to the n leaves two to the n, which grows without bound.
So no constant works. An exponent multiplies the base. It isn't a constant factor.
Logarithm bases are different... they only differ by a constant.

lines: Little o means strictly slower.
For every constant, f eventually falls below it.
When the ratio has a limit, zero means little o... a positive constant means Theta... and infinity means little omega.
But the limit may not exist. So the ratio test is sufficient... not necessary.
Here's the most common slip.
Big O is not worst case.
A case picks a function. For insertion sort, sorted input costs seven comparisons, random about nineteen, reversed twenty eight... that's eight items, checked over every order.
A bound then relates that function to another.
So best case Theta of n and worst case Theta of n squared are both exact.
Two axes. Don't mix them up.
A quicksort that always pivots on the first key does almost five hundred thousand comparisons on a thousand sorted keys.
Pick the pivot at random instead. How many comparisons do you expect on that same sorted input?
answer: About ten thousand nine hundred eighty six. The same as for any other order.
Average case assumes a distribution over inputs... and can be wrong when real inputs aren't like it.
Expected time uses the algorithm's own coin flips... so it holds for every fixed input.

lines: Two thousand runs, one thousand keys.
The mean is about eleven thousand. The slowest run, fifteen thousand.
An expectation allows rare slow runs.
With high probability says something stronger... the chance of failure is at most one over n to the c, and you pick c.
Services are judged on tails. So ask which one you're being given.
Does a list of a thousand distinct numbers contain a duplicate?
Compare every pair... almost five hundred thousand steps, and no extra storage.
Heapsort in place, then one scan... about eighteen thousand.
Or a hash set... a thousand lookups, but a thousand values stored.
Time bought with space. Always say which two resources, and what you count.
Asymptotics describe growth... not speed at one size.
A hundred n beats n squared only from a hundred up.
Below that, the worse algorithm wins.
Where constants and cache behaviour decide, measure.
One more trap.
Trial division is order square root of the value... sixty five thousand steps for a thirty two bit prime.
Double the bits... and it's over four billion.
In the length of the input, that's exponential.
A cost polynomial in the value, but exponential in the bit length, is called pseudo-polynomial.
Now, a feel for the ladder at a million items.
Log n is about twenty steps. N log n takes two hundredths of a second.
N squared takes a thousand seconds... nearly seventeen minutes.
And two to the n is hopeless by sixty four... centuries.
Those step counts assume a machine model. That's next.
Seven things to keep.
Inequalities with witnesses. Strict little o and little omega. Bound is not case. Average is not expected.
High probability is a tail. Time trades with space. And n is the size in bits.
Next, the machine model behind the step counts.
